title: Quadratics with Complex Solutions
short: A negative discriminant gives two complex conjugate solutions.

blocks.html: Now the The Quadratic Formula never fails. When the discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$ is negative, its square root is imaginary, and the formula hands you two complex solutions. You have the tools from Adding and Multiplying Complex Numbers to simplify them.
If $b^2 - 4ac < 0$, the solutions of $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ are $x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$ with $\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac} = \sqrt{4ac - b^2}\,i$. They form a conjugate pair $p + qi$ and $p - qi$.

The formula comes from completing the square, which never needed the discriminant to be positive. When it is negative, the $\pm$ adds and subtracts the same imaginary amount from the same real number $-\frac{b}{2a}$, so the two answers are conjugates. On the graph this means the parabola never touches the $x$-axis: there are no real zeros, but the equation still has two solutions off the real line.

blocks.name: parabola
blocks.cap: $y = x^2 - 2x + 5$ floats above the $x$-axis, so it has no real zeros. Its solutions are $1 + 2i$ and $1 - 2i$.

blocks.name: complexplane
blocks.cap: The two solutions $1 \pm 2i$ are mirror images across the real axis: complex conjugates.

blocks.title: A root that does not simplify

blocks.html: Stopping at "no solution." That answer is right only if the question asks for real solutions. Another slip is dividing only one term by $2a$: in $\frac{2 \pm 4i}{2}$ both the 2 and the $4i$ get divided, giving $1 \pm 2i$, not $1 \pm 4i$.
